lesson.title: Turning the Volume Up and Down: Enhancers and Silencers
lesson.summary: Enhancers and silencers are DNA regulatory sequences, distinct from the promoter itself, that increase or decrease a gene's transcription rate, often from a surprising distance.
lesson.body:
The promoter is where RNA polymerase II and the general transcription factors assemble to start reading a gene, but on its own the promoter only supports a low, baseline level of transcription. Real cells need much more precise control than that: a liver cell needs a metabolic gene blasting at full volume, while a skin cell needs that same gene almost silent. That fine control comes from two other kinds of DNA sequences, enhancers and silencers, which sit apart from the promoter and tune transcription up or down.

An enhancer is a DNA sequence that, when bound by activator transcription factors, increases the rate of transcription at a target gene. What makes enhancers unusual is that they do not have to sit right next to the gene they control. An enhancer can be located thousands of base pairs upstream or downstream of its target, inside an intron, or even on the far side of a neighboring gene, and it can work in either orientation. This works because DNA is flexible enough to loop back on itself: when activator proteins bind the distant enhancer, the loop brings them into direct physical contact with the Mediator complex and general transcription factors sitting at the promoter, effectively closing the genomic distance and boosting the rate at which RNA polymerase II starts new transcripts.

A silencer works the same way in reverse. It is a DNA sequence that, when bound by repressor proteins, decreases transcription of the target gene, either by blocking activators from doing their job or by interfering with assembly of the transcription machinery at the promoter. Like enhancers, silencers can act at a distance and are separate elements from the promoter itself.

The payoff of this system is combinatorial control. A single promoter can be paired with different sets of enhancers and silencers in different cell types, and since transcription factor availability differs from cell to cell, the same gene can be strongly activated in one tissue and firmly repressed in another, all without changing the gene's sequence or its promoter. This modularity is a big part of how a genome with a limited number of genes can still produce the enormous diversity of cell types found in a complex organism, and it sets the stage for the next layer of control: epigenetic mechanisms that make expression patterns stable and heritable across cell divisions.
